title: The Rule of the Vital Few
subtitle: An Italian man looked at who owned the land in his country. He found a strange pattern — and today people call it the 80/20 rule.
intention: you'll learn where the 80/20 rule comes from, use it on a real problem, and practise most, a few, a lot of and other words for quantity.
warmup: Do you wear all your clothes, or only a few favourites?
How many apps on your phone do you really use?
Which part of your week is the most useful?

vocab.heading: A · What does the word mean? Guess from the sentence
vocab.intro: Read the sentence. Say what the word in bold means. Then check.

items.sent: The game was not equal: one team scored nine goals and the other scored none. The result was very uneven.
items.meaning: uneven — not the same on both sides; not equal.

items.sent: Only a few people came to the meeting — five or six.
The shop checks every phone for problems before it sells it.
items.meaning: problem — something that is wrong or not working.

items.sent: Water and sleep are necessary for life.

vocab.heading: B · Which word is it?
vocab.intro: The words are: rich · complaint · owner. Read the meaning and say the word.

items.sent: (noun) When a customer says that something is wrong.
items.meaning: complaint — “The café had ten complaints about slow service.”

items.sent: (noun) The person who has something — a house, a shop, a car.
items.meaning: owner — “The owner of the restaurant is very friendly.”
rich — “A small number of families were very rich.”

vocab.heading: C · One word for all three
vocab.intro: One word fits all three phrases. Say the word.

items.sent: ___ of my time  ·  ___ people agree  ·  ___ of the money

vocab_use: Which few things give you most of your free time?
Have you ever made a complaint in a shop or a restaurant?
Is your country's money spread evenly, or is it uneven?

story.heading: Part 1 — The man who counted
paras: Vilfredo Pareto was born in Paris in 1848. His father was Italian, his mother was French. First he was an engineer: he worked with trains and with metal. He was clever, and he loved to argue about politics.
Then, when he was about forty-five, he changed his job completely. He became an economist — a person who studies money — at a university in Switzerland.
At that time, people argued a lot about money: who has it, and who should have it. Pareto did something different. He did not argue. He collected numbers about land and money in different countries.
checks: What did he do that was different?
answers: He was an engineer (trains and metal).
An economist — a person who studies money.
He collected real numbers instead of only arguing.
story.discuss: Is it better to argue with opinions or with numbers? Why?

story.heading: Part 2 — A strange pattern
paras: The numbers surprised him. In country after country, the picture was the same and very uneven: a small number of people owned most of the land and most of the money.
The famous version of the story says this: in Italy, 20% of the people owned 80% of the land.
Many books add a nice story about his garden: 20% of his pea plants gave him 80% of the peas. It is a lovely story, but there is no good evidence for it. It is probably not true.
Pareto wrote about money. He died in 1923, long before anybody said the words “the 80/20 rule”.
checks: What is the famous version of the story?
answers: A small number of people had most of the land and money.
In Italy, 20% of people owned 80% of the land.
Probably not — there is no good evidence.
story.discuss: Why do people like the garden story so much?

story.heading: Part 3 — The few that matter
paras: Fifty years later, an American engineer called Joseph Juran worked in a big factory. His job was to check products for problems.
He noticed something. The problems were uneven too. A few causes made most of the problems. If the factory fixed those few causes first, most of the problems disappeared.

Juran needed a name for this idea. He remembered Pareto's numbers, and he called it the Pareto principle: the vital few and the useful many. Later, he said honestly that Pareto had never said this about everything — he had only written about money.
Today people use the rule everywhere: in shops, in sport, in schools. But remember: it is a helpful guide, not a law. Sometimes it is 70/30, sometimes 90/10.
checks: What did Juran notice in the factory?
What name did he give the idea?
answers: A few causes made most of the problems.
The Pareto principle — “the vital few and the useful many”.
story.discuss: Where do you see this pattern in your life?

tool_tab.lead: Put your problems in order, from big to small. The bars show how many. The red line adds them up. The first few bars are usually most of the problem — the vital few.
how: Count something real: problems, complaints, hours, money.
Put the causes in order: the biggest first.
Add the numbers until you have about 80 out of 100.
Fix those first. Then count again — the picture will be different.

sort.intro: A small shop had 200 returns (people bringing things back) last month. Which causes are the vital few — the big ones — and which are the small many?

items.text: The customer changed their mind — 12 returns

items.why: 16 of 200 — not in the top two.

items.text: The colour was different on the website — 50 returns

items.why: only 2 — but if it is dangerous, fix it anyway!

breaks: It is not a law. Don't push your numbers into 80/20.
Small can be serious. One dangerous problem is more important than a hundred small ones.
Be careful with people. “Most of our money comes from a few customers” can mean a shop stops caring about everybody else.
discuss: What are the “vital few” in your work or your studies?
When is this rule a bad idea?

grammar.name: most, a few, a lot of
grammar.lead: This rule is about how many and how much. These are the words you need.
notes:
Countable things (chairs, people, problems): a few, many, a lot of, most.
“A few customers complained.”  “Most people agree.”

Uncountable things (water, money, time, information): a little, much, a lot of, most.
“I have a little time.”  “Most of the money went on rent.”

a few = some (it's OK).  few = not many (it's a problem).
“I have a few friends here.” 🙂  “I have few friends here.” 🙁

most or most of?
General: “Most students have a phone.”  This group: “Most of the students in my class have a phone.”
Careful: use much mainly in questions and negatives. “I don't have much time.”  “Do you drink much coffee?”

exercises.heading: Choose the right word
exercises.intro: Write a few, a little, most, many or much.
items: 1. ___ of the complaints were about slow service — about eighty per cent.
2. There is only ___ milk left. We need to buy some.
3. I don't have ___ time today. Can we meet tomorrow?
5. How ___ students are there in your class?

exercises.heading: Read the café chart
exercises.intro: Look at the café chart in The Tool tab. Complete the sentences.
items: 1. ___ of the complaints (50 of 100) were about slow service.
2. Only ___ complaints were about parking — four.
3. Two problems together made ___ of the complaints.
4. There were not ___ complaints about Wi-Fi.

grammar.closing: Now describe your week: what takes most of your time, and what takes only a little?

speak.intro: Now use the rule in your life. Choose a task and speak. You can start the timer.
speak.useful: “Most of my …” · “Only a few …” · “I spend a lot of time on …” · “I don't have much …”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Your vital few
paras: Which few things give you most of your results at work or in study?

tasks.label: Task 2 — Your problems
paras: Think of something that often goes wrong for you. What causes most of it?

tasks.label: Task 3 — Your things
paras: Look around your home. Which few things do you use every day? Which do you never use?

final: If a few friends give you most of your happy times, what does that tell you?
Should a shop give more time to its best customers? Is that fair?
Can a simple rule be useful even when it is not exactly true?
From memory: make four sentences with most, a few, a lot of and not much.
